chunks: "I'd split it into loss and distortion. Loss is the signal getting smaller as it travels.

The sources are conductor loss, which is resistance that grows as square root of f from the skin effect and gets worse with rough copper; dielectric loss, which grows about linearly with frequency from the loss tangent of the laminate; and radiation, small for stripline but real at discontinuities.
Reflections also steal energy from the main wave at every impedance step: vias, connectors, stubs, pads. Distortion comes from the fact that the loss isn't flat.

The channel attenuates high frequencies more than low ones, so a sharp edge loses its high-frequency content and smears out; dispersion also means different frequency components arrive at slightly different times.
In the time domain that's ISI: the tail of one bit lands on the next one, and the eye closes. Reflections add their own ghost copies of the signal.

To minimize it: shorter traces, wider traces, smoother copper, a low-loss laminate instead of FR-4, stripline instead of microstrip for radiation, clean impedance control, back-drilled vias, good connectors.

Then compensate actively: transmit pre-emphasis or de-emphasis boosts the high frequencies up front, the receiver uses a CTLE to flatten the channel and a DFE to cancel the post-cursor ISI, and if the channel is just too long I'd put in a retimer."
